III. Details of the Photodector Fabrication and Characterization

This GaN based UV photodetector was grown on a sapphire substrate using a horizontal flow low-pressure metalorganic chemical vapor deposition (MOCVD) reactor at a growth pressure of 10 ~ 100 mbar and temperature of ~1000 °C. A p-i-n configuration was used for the detector structure where silicon was used for the n- type dopant and magnesium for the p- type dopant. Metal contacts were achieved using a Ti/Au bilayer for the n- type ohmic contact and a Ni/Au bilayer for the p- type ohmic contact. The overall detector structure is shown in Figure 3. A technique known as lateral epitaxial overgrowth was used to dramatically reduce the number of defects in the template used as the foundation for the growth of the GaN p-i-n detector. This was accomplished by first growing up from the substrate through etched SiO₂ channels then growing horizontally due to the preferential GaN crystal formation on the horizontal plane⁶,⁷ (Fig. 4).
Fig. 4 General structure for a material grown by lateral epitaxial overgrowth (LEO)

The measured peak responsivity of the detector was 200 mA/W at 362 nm. This corresponds to an external quantum efficiency of 69% (Fig. 5); and taking into account surface absorption and scattering, an estimated internal quantum efficiency of ~86%. Figure 5 shows that the responsivity of the GaN detector decreases by approximately 5 orders-of-magnitude for wavelengths greater than ~365 nm. This means there is virtually no detection of electromagnetic radiation from about 365 nm up into the visible light region making the detector

visible blind. The response of the detector does not perfectly follow the erythemal weighting function at longer wavelengths (greater than ~365 nm). At these wavelengths, the GaN detector shows a flat response whereas the erythemal weighting function shows a declining response. Incorporating aluminum into the GaN photodetector structure would allow one to design an active region which would more closely follow the erythemal weighting function. The feasibility of this approach has already been demonstrated.⁸

IV. Details of the Associated Electronics and Software

The portable UV detection device consists primarily of the GaN detector, a multi-stage operational amplifier (op-amp) circuit, a microcontroller circuit, and a liquid-crystal display (LCD) module (Fig. 6). The photocurrent generated by the detector is fed through the multi-stage transimpedance amplifier to boost the signal into the millivolt range (Fig. 7). High-precision OPA277 op-amps were used for the gain circuit. The first stage of the amplifier circuit converts the current signal to a voltage signal, while the second and third stages provide dynamic gain. The dynamic gain is exponentially varied over four orders-of-magnitude using a digital potentiometer controlled by the 16F873 peripheral interface controller (PIC). For simplicity, the gain is divided into powers of two to allow the PIC microcontroller to continually adjust the gain in order to keep at least 6 bits of resolution in the internal analog to digital converter (ADC).

The 16F873 PIC microcontroller used in this device runs at 19.66 MHz with an instruction time of only 200 ns. The code for this controller is 1,200 lines, which compiles to approximately 500 14-bit instruction words. The code is divided into a main loop, which handles detector sampling and the user interface, and an interrupt driven routine used to keep accurate time.
